cards.explanation: The answer is understanding to learn God's commandments. The psalmist says, “give me understanding to learn Your commandments.” Notice he doesn't ask for a shortcut. He asks for the kind of understanding that lets him learn them, and a good student goes straight to the Maker for that.
The missing word is “word.” The psalmist says, “…for I have hoped in Your word.” His hope is in what God has said. That's a sturdy place to put your weight, friends.

The answer is True. The psalmist says, “…in faithfulness You have afflicted me.” That's a hard thing to say out loud, and he says it right next to “I know, O LORD, that Your judgments are righteous…” He calls the LORD faithful even in the hard season, and I think that took real honesty.

The answer is that he wants to live. The psalmist says, “May Your compassion come to me, that I may live…” He's asking for compassion so that he may live, and I think he knows he needs it. Then he gives his reason in the same verse, which comes up in the next question.

The missing word is delight. The psalmist says, “…for Your law is my delight.” Some people hear the word law and picture a chore list. For this psalmist it's the thing he enjoys. Now THAT is a different outlook, friends.

The answer is that he will meditate on God's precepts. The psalmist says, “I will meditate on Your precepts.” The arrogant are subverting him with a lie, and his move is to think deeply on what God has said. He doesn't spend that verse planning anything against them.

The answer is False. The psalmist says, “May those who fear You turn to me, those who know Your testimonies.” He's asking for those people to come near him, not walk off. After all the liars in this stretch, I think he wants some good company.

The answer is so he won't be put to shame. The verse gives the reason itself: “May my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame.” The heart comes first, and the shame is what he hopes to avoid. He's asking about the inside, not just the outside.

The answer is “When will You comfort me?” That's what the psalmist asks while his eyes are looking for God's promise. It's an honest question, asked straight to the LORD. And being honest like that is something this psalm does over and over.

The answer is False. The psalmist says, “Though I am like a wineskin dried up by smoke, I do not forget Your statutes.” He compares himself to a wineskin dried up by smoke, and he still says he does not forget. I bet that comparison means he's feeling worn out, but the verse itself only gives us the picture.

The answer is when God will judge his persecutors. The psalmist asks, “How many days must Your servant wait? When will You execute judgment on my persecutors?” The first question is about the waiting, and the second is about his persecutors. He's bringing both to the LORD instead of keeping them inside.

The answer is that there's no cause for it at all. The psalmist says, “I am persecuted without cause—help me!” Without cause means the persecution isn't justified. And he says it right after calling all of God's commandments faithful, which I think is a heavy thing to carry.

The answer is True. The psalmist says, “They almost wiped me from the earth, but I have not forsaken Your precepts.” They came close, and he still held on. That little word “but” is carrying a lot, friends.

The two missing words are revive and obey. First, the psalmist prays, “Revive me according to Your loving devotion…” He's asking for new life, measured by God's loving devotion. Then he says, “…that I may obey the testimony of Your mouth.” The reviving has a purpose, and the prayer goes from new life to following God's word.

The answer is that God's word is everlasting and fixed in the heavens. The psalmist says, “Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens.” Everlasting and firmly fixed. That's a lot of staying power in one verse.
The answer is False. The psalmist says, “You established the earth, and it endures.” The first half of the statement is true, but the second half isn't. God established the earth, and it endures.

The missing word is servants. The psalmist says, “Your ordinances stand to this day, for all things are servants to You.” All things, not just some of them. That's a big sentence, and he says it plainly.

The answer is that he would have perished in his affliction. The psalmist says, “If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction.” He's looking back at the hard stretch and naming what he says kept him from perishing. I think that's a heavy thing to say.

The answer is True. The psalmist says, “I will never forget Your precepts, for by them You have revived me.” Revived means given new life. He's saying God did it through those precepts, and that's why he won't forget them.

The answer is that he asks the LORD to save him. The psalmist says, “I am Yours; save me, for I have sought Your precepts.” He starts with who he belongs to, and then he asks. That order matters, friends.

The answer is False. The psalmist says, “I have seen a limit to all perfection, but Your commandment is without limit.” The limit belongs to all perfection that he has seen. God's commandment is without limit. (Psalm 119:96)
